A_target.statement:
Let $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \R_{>0}$ be [[Definition:Strictly Positive Real Number|strictly positive real numbers]].
Then:
:$\displaystyle \frac {x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n} n \ge \paren {x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n}^{1 / n}$

B_source.statement:
Let $\phi$ be a [[Definition:Concave Real Function|concave real function]] on an [[Definition:Real Interval|interval]] $I$.
Let $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in I$ and let $w_1, \ldots, w_n \ge 0$ with $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n w_i = 1$.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \map \phi {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n w_i x_i} \ge \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n w_i \map \phi {x_i}$

derived.the inequality for the average: the logarithm of the arithmetic mean is at least the average of the logarithms
derived.exponentiating both sides: the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean

validity_conditions: The logarithm is concave on the positive reals, since its second derivative is negative there, so Jensen applies with phi the logarithm.
The numbers must be strictly positive for the logarithm to be defined, which matches the hypothesis of the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality.
Exponentiation is increasing, so it preserves the direction of the inequality and converts the average of logarithms into the geometric mean.
proof_plan:
From [[Logarithm is Strictly Concave]], $\ln$ is [[Definition:Concave Real Function|concave]] on $\R_{>0}$.
Apply [[Jensen's Inequality (Real Analysis)|Jensen's inequality]] with $\phi = \ln$ and $w_i = \dfrac 1 n$.

This gives:
:$\displaystyle \map \ln {\frac 1 n \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i} \ge \frac 1 n \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \ln x_i$
